▸ The death of web development education – Rescuing a field from disappearing

💡 Generative AI threatens web development education, necessitating industry compensation for human educators to sustain technical learning pipelines.

Generative AI is severely destabilizing web development education by diverting learners from structured, human-led instruction toward error-prone chatbots. Uncompensated LLM scraping and heavy crawler bandwidth costs are driving technical authors offline, effectively destroying the economic model for free, high-quality programming tutorials. Furthermore, this shift degrades technical literacy by replacing peer collaboration with subtly inaccurate AI outputs while incurring massive environmental and financial costs for tasks often achievable through traditional non-AI automation. Ultimately, sustaining the software engineering pipeline requires meaningful industry support and compensation for technical educators rather than passive demands for them to adapt.

📝 关键要点 (7 sections)
  • Erosion of Developer Education: Generative AI has fundamentally disrupted traditional web development training, driving learners away from human-crafted courses toward error-prone chatbots.
  • Exploitative Scraping Destroys Monetization: Prominent technical authors are taking their content offline as AI crawlers consume bandwidth without generating ad revenue or book sales.
  • Decline of Human Community: Chatbots and social media algorithms are replacing authentic peer collaboration and intentional teaching, leading many experienced educators to burn out or step back.
  • Disincentivizing Open Content Creation: Educational creators face severe revenue losses because LLMs scrape their work without compensation, eliminating the financial motivation to produce free programming tutorials.
  • Flawed Quality and Shifted Labor: AI-generated text often introduces subtle inaccuracies, shifting the burden of fact-checking and editing from original authors onto editors and readers.
  • Questioning AI Productivity Gains: Many supposed AI productivity boosts could be accomplished through standard non-AI automations without incurring high financial, environmental, and human costs.
  • Dismissive Industry Responses: Telling affected educators to simply adapt ignores the catastrophic impact on tech education, highlighting a desperate need for industry empathy and support.

▸ Think local

💡 Developers should shift to local, open-source LLMs to escape rising cloud costs and ensure sustainable software independence.

Although software development remains the most viable practical domain for LLMs, the current low token pricing is heavily subsidized by big tech and bound for an economic correction that will inevitably push centralized models toward high-paying enterprise clients. To adapt, developers should pivot away from speculative commercialization and prioritize building quiet, hyper-local utility tools while ensuring they fully understand the code they generate. Ultimately, adopting open, locally run models—which only need to reach a "good enough" performance threshold for personal workflows—decouples development from corporate cloud dependencies and secures a sustainable, independent future for personal software.

  • Personal Software Ethos: Building AI-assisted software should focus on quiet, home-cooked utility for personal use rather than public distribution or seeking glory.

  • Enterprise AI Pivot: As consumer markets become unsustainable for centralized LLMs, providers will pivot toward high-paying corporate clients, leaving mainstream users behind.
  • Rise of Local Models: Open, locally run AI models do not need to match massive data centers, as achieving a 'good enough' threshold is sufficient for personal software development.
  • Reclaiming Technological Agency: Decoupling LLM technology from centralized corporate power enables a future where locally run, personal software projects can flourish independently.

💡 A follow-up benchmark shows LLMs still fail simple deterministic tasks by hallucinating answers, requiring constant manual verification.

A one-year follow-up benchmark evaluating leading LLMs on a deterministic set-intersection task—matching top-level domains (TLDs) to valid HTML5 elements—showed that most models still fail despite recent technical advancements. Models exhibited superficial reasoning by hallucinating tags, missing standard elements like `<data>`, padding outputs with irrelevant "near misses," and ignoring technical edge cases such as Punycode TLDs and embedded MathML. In contrast, Siri successfully provided the correct answer only by bypassing generative modeling to directly retrieve data from an existing web page via traditional search. Ultimately, the test demonstrates that LLMs frequently produce confident, plausible-sounding filler for simple factual lookups, reinforcing that they require constant manual verification unlike deterministic tools.

  • Retesting LLM Performance: The author re-evaluated leading AI models one year after an initial benchmark to test if they improved on a straightforward set-intersection question. Despite technical advancements, most models still failed to provide accurate results.

  • Hallucinations and Inaccuracies: Models like Gemini Flash hallucinated non-existent TLDs and HTML tags, while reasoning models missed standard tags like `<data>` and `search`. Other models padded responses with irrelevant 'near misses' to appear thorough.
  • Siri's Surprising Win: Siri successfully provided the correct answer, but only because it directly retrieved data from an existing web page. This highlights how traditional web search can beat generative LLMs on factual lookup tasks.
  • Unhandled Technical Nuances: Models completely overlooked edge cases like Punycode TLDs matching valid HTML custom elements and allowed embedded MathML tags. These technical omissions demonstrate the superficial nature of LLM reasoning.
  • Risks of AI Sycophancy: LLMs often generate confident, plausible-sounding filler that misleads uncritical users into accepting incorrect data. Unlike deterministic tools like spreadsheets, LLMs require constant manual verification.
